diagrams.cap: Rectifier raises DC voltage above the inverter's; current flows from the higher to the lower. Reversing both converter voltages reverses power flow.

formulas.name: HVDC links
notes: Tip: Back-to-back ties grids of different frequencies (asynchronous link).

formulas.name: When HVDC wins
notes: Tip: No skin effect, no stability limit, 2 conductors — but costly converters and harmonic filters.

why.cause: long distance → HVDC cheaper beyond the break-even length
why.effect: DC line carries no reactive power (converters still absorb Q), no skin effect, only 2 conductors; ~600–800 km overhead, ~50 km cable.
Power flows from the higher DC voltage end.

why.cause: converters create harmonics (6k ± 1 on the AC side)
why.effect: AC and DC filters are needed.

why.cause: converters absorb reactive power → capacitor banks at both ends
no synchronism needed → can link 50 Hz and 60 Hz grids

mcqs.q: Q1. Dominant AC-side harmonics of a 6-pulse converter
Q2. A line-commutated converter works as an inverter when α is
mcqs.ans: Ans: (a) Above 90° V<sub>d</sub> ∝ cos α becomes negative for α > 90°.
Ans: (b) Long lines, submarine cables and asynchronous links No reactive charging current and no stability limit.

mcqs.q: Q4. Do HVDC converters consume reactive power?
mcqs.ans: Ans: (c) Yes — both rectifier and inverter Current lags voltage by about α (or γ); filters and capacitors supply it.
